implementation_notes: ScalaMock is the native Scala mocking framework: inside a MockFactory the test creates a double with stub[Service1] when only canned answers matter and mock[Service2] when calls must be expected, then configures per-call behaviour with (mock.getUserName _).expects(42).returns("John") - or returnsZIO(...) for effectful returns - and verifies with verify(mock.method _).once(). That expectation DSL is the configuration interface, generated by macros from the trait, so no double class is written and the trait's signature stays compiler-checked. Integrations exist for ScalaTest, specs2, ZIO Test and cats-effect, and ScalaMock 7 supports Scala 2.12, 2.13 and 3 on the JVM.
pitfalls: The underscore syntax ((mock.method _).expects(...)) is mandatory for methods with arguments, and forgetting it produces confusing type errors or silently unexpected behaviour.
stub mocks are permissive while mock expectations are verified, so mixing the two in one test hides calls that were never expected.
Macro-based mocking depends on the Scala version; a project moving to Scala 3 needs the matching ScalaMock release (7.x) rather than the 4.x line.

variants.name: Hand-written trait implementation with configurable values
variants.idiom_name: hand-written class implementing the trait with configurable vals
variants.implementation_notes: A class or case class implements the collaborator trait and returns whatever it was configured with (a constructor value, a var, or a function-valued field), which is the classic structure written directly in Scala and works with any test framework - MUnit, ZIO Test, ScalaTest - without macro-generated mocks. Prefer it when the double must implement real behaviour, when the trait uses opaque or inline types that macro mocking struggles with, or when the test wants the double to be a plain value it can inspect. Scala's function values make the functional variant of the same idea a one-liner.
variants.code_sketch:
trait Clock:
  def now(): Instant

final class ConfigurableClock(var answer: () => Instant) extends Clock:
  def now(): Instant = answer()

val clock = ConfigurableClock(() => throw TimeoutException())
pitfalls: A var-configured fake is mutable state; putting it in a shared fixture lets one test's configuration leak into the next.

Traits with context-bound or effectful return types (F[A]) cannot be faked by a simple value: the fake must lift answers into the effect, which is where the mocking framework's returnsZIO/returnsF helpers pay off.
Because nothing verifies the fake against the real implementation, missing members or wrong semantics are caught only by the compiler.
